answer: Genesis begins with God only as an old tradition; the heavens and the earth were already there on their own, and God simply arranged what existed, so creation does not depend on Him at all.
Genesis presents the patriarchs as flawless heroes who never failed, and that is why God chose them: their moral perfection earned the covenant that rests upon their goodness.
Biblical dominion gives humans full ownership of creation, so we may use it however we like; stewardship is a modern idea, and no higher Owner will ever ask us to account for it.
The serpent was actually defending God's word and showing His goodness; he never questioned what God said, and the temptation shows the command was unclear and that God was generous.
Romans 5 teaches that Adam and Christ are equal and opposite forces, so the fall was never really answered, and Christ brings no greater grace than Adam's sin brought ruin.
The repeated phrase "and he died" teaches that death is natural and was never a consequence of sin, and Enoch's being taken proves nothing about God's power over death.
To walk with God means occasional bursts of religious feeling in a crisis; Enoch shows that steady daily faith, obedience and dependence on God are unnecessary for pleasing Him.
Abraham's faith was merely agreeing with facts about God while his life stayed the same; his departure was a payment that bought the promise, and obedience played no real part.
The delay shows that waiting is pointless and that people should arrange the promise themselves; Sarah's plan with Hagar was the faithful way to receive what God had promised.
The ram was not a substitute for Isaac; Abraham offered it as a gift for his own sake, and no life was given in anyone's place, so the story has nothing to do with sacrifice and substitution.
God made a brand new covenant with Isaac that had nothing to do with Abraham; its foundation was Isaac's own ability, and the promises of presence, land and blessing to the nations were withdrawn.
Jacob felt no fear at all about Esau, he trusted entirely in his own planning, and he did not pray; the gifts and the camps show that prayer was unnecessary.
Jacob's favoritism fully excuses the brothers, since a favored child provokes violence and nobody in that family bears any responsibility for what they chose to do.
Joseph's promotion proves a prosperity formula: whoever stays faithful will always be rewarded with visible success and quick promotion, and God guarantees it to everyone who obeys.
Egypt was the final covenant destination, since the promises of Genesis were fulfilled when the family settled in Goshen, and Canaan was never really given to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Human beings can reach God by their own cleverness and effort, so self-disclosure is unnecessary; if God stayed hidden we could still know Him fully by climbing up to Him through reason.
Illumination is the Spirit causing the Bible to be written, and inspiration is the Spirit helping believers understand it today; the two are the same work, once finished and never repeated.
God's immutability means He changes His essence, character and promises whenever circumstances change, so Malachi 3:6 teaches that the Lord is constantly different from what He was.
Jesus ascended because He abandoned His people; He sits at the right hand of the Father to rest, not to intercede, and He could not send the Holy Spirit unless He stayed on earth.
Regeneration is something the sinner accomplishes by his own decision, since total depravity leaves him alive and able to give himself spiritual life without any work of the Spirit.
Dignity and depravity cannot both be true; because humans are totally depraved they have lost all worth, and because they have dignity they have no real sin touching any part of them.
Christ is called the last Adam because He too disobeyed under pressure; His failure, like Adam's, brings guilt on His people, and the image of God is therefore never restored in them.
A sin of omission is doing wrong actively, such as lying, and a sin of commission is failing to act; but only commission counts before God, and leaving good undone is never really sin.
Salvation is a reward paid to the righteous for their goodness; God saves those who deserve it, and it is not a gift for the guilty who have earned nothing.
The church's mission points in only one direction, outward to evangelism; worship and fellowship are distractions, and a healthy church should drop the upward and inward dimensions entirely.
Unity requires uniformity: the Bible calls for one body only if all believers worship and practice identically, so denominational differences prove that Christians are not truly united.
The Kingdom of God is only future; God's reign has not begun and is not at work among His people now, and nothing of it has broken into the world until the end.
John 18:36 teaches that Christ's reign works by earthly political power and competes for a throne in the ordinary way, so His followers should fight to win control of nations.
Ezra set his heart first to teach the Law, then to practice it, and only last to study it; the order does not matter, since a pastor can teach before he has studied or obeyed.

Exegesis means reading your own meaning into the text, and eisegesis means drawing the author's meaning out of it; every pastor should choose eisegesis on Monday because the author's intent does not matter.
The lesson says a pastor should apply the passage first, and only afterwards pray, read it, study the context and compare other Scripture; application comes before understanding.
The absence of God's name in Esther shows that God is not present or active in the book at all; the events happen by chance, and no providence lies behind the insomnia or the banquets.
On the Emmaus road Jesus avoided the Scriptures and explained everything through His own authority; the lesson says Moses and the Prophets have nothing to say about Christ.
The lesson recommends that a pastor avoid cross-references, never use a concordance, and read only the passage he is preaching so that Scripture is not compared with Scripture.
The signals show that each detail of a parable is an allegory with its own hidden meaning, so the interpreter should ignore the audience and the climax and decode every small element.
The raising of Lazarus is purely a historical event with no teaching; the miracle is separate from the sermon, and Jesus preached nothing through it about resurrection or life.
In Hosea's marriage Gomer represents God, the faithful partner, and Hosea represents unfaithful Israel; the slave market shows that Israel bought God back.
Literal and literalistic are exactly the same thing; to interpret literally is to flatten every phrase to bare physical meaning, so "I am the door" means Jesus is made of wood.
The diagnostic questions tell the pastor to always read each text in a flat literal way, never ask whether it is a figure of speech, and ignore what the speaker meant.
Reni's painting shows that the Father is already perfectly clear without Christ, and that the mirror is unnecessary since we can see the Father directly without looking at Christ.
Mocking is named the most dangerous response because the mocker can never be argued with; delay is harmless because the one who delays has made no decision and so cannot be lost.
The gospel spread in the first century in spite of the world and not because of any preparation; the Greek language, the Roman roads and the synagogues all hindered it and delayed Christ's coming.
There was nothing unique about the first-century pulpit; later preachers have the same eyewitness experience of walking with Jesus and the same direct revelation as Paul had.
Tertullian gave Eastern theology its Greek vocabulary and rejected the word Trinity; Justin Martyr wrote no defense at all, and none of the apologists answered the pagan charges.
The Edict of Milan in 313 made Christianity illegal and confiscated church property, which ended freedom of worship and began a new age of persecution under Constantine.
Nicaea in 325 agreed with Arius that the Son was a created being, and Chalcedon in 451 declared that Christ had only one nature, which settled the Christological question.
Augustine taught that sinners are born neutral with a free will able to choose God unaided, so grace does not come first and faith is not a gift from God.
Gregory is called the first medieval pope because he refused any role in governing Rome; he left the city to the Lombards and the bishop of Rome never became a political authority.
In Anselm's theory the atonement was a ransom paid to the devil, and sin did not offend God's justice at all, so no satisfaction and no God-man were needed.
The forerunners were honored and protected by the church, which welcomed their message; Hus was released with a safe-conduct, so the institution always stood with the gospel.

In the tower Luther concluded that righteousness is something we earn by confession and penance; he learned from Romans 1:17 that God's righteousness is a standard that condemns us and only our works save.
The Council of Trent accepted the Protestant doctrine of justification by faith alone and abolished the sale of indulgences without defending any traditional Catholic teaching.
German Pietism rejected Bible reading and prayer groups, and Francke's Halle abandoned orphans and missions; Spener wanted a colder and more intellectual church.
Carey agreed with the hyper-Calvinists that the Great Commission was given only to the apostles, and he wrote that Christians had no duty to use means to spread the gospel.
Psalm 1 is called the threshold psalm because it teaches that there is no real choice between ways; the wicked and the righteous end up in the same place, so the reader need not decide.
Psalm 1 says the wicked stand firmly rooted in the judgment and their way endures forever, like a tree, while the righteous are the chaff that the wind blows away.
Psalm 23 promises that believers will never go through the valley at all; God removes every giant and every hardship in advance, as He did for David, so we are always spared the shadow of death.
The first attempt failed because David lacked enough men; carrying the Ark on a new ox cart was exactly what God commanded, and the story teaches that how we approach God does not matter.
God never confronts anyone with sin today; the conscience is unreliable, hardship is only random bad luck, and Christian friends should never speak to us about wrongdoing.
Psalm 119 is among the shortest chapters in the Bible and has no particular structure at all; it is a loose collection of unrelated verses with no acrostic pattern.
Psalm 119:97 teaches that religion is a burden to be endured from duty; the psalmist merely obeys the law without loving it, and his mind avoids the Word whenever possible.
The cry of Psalm 22:1 was only a figure of speech, since the Father never forsook the Son; the nails and the mockery were the deepest pain, and no sin was borne in that moment.
Satan succeeded in destroying the Righteous Seed when Athaliah killed the royal line and Herod slaughtered the infants, so God's plan failed and the cross and resurrection never happened.
The paralyzed man asked for the hymn so he could number his troubles instead of his blessings, and that sets up Psalm 103 as a psalm of complaint that tells us to forget His benefits.
The renewal of strength in Psalm 103 is the world's search for youth, a promise that believers will stay physically young; Isaiah's eagle promise has nothing to do with waiting on the LORD.
The capstone units shift away from ministry back to asking only what a psalm means; the Psalms are no different from the rest of Scripture, where God speaks to us and never the reverse.
The lesson warns that ministers should let private devotion shrink as their public skill grows, because a tree needs no hidden roots to bear fruit and public ability is enough.
Apologia means an apology in the sense of saying sorry for the faith, and Peter teaches that believers have no duty to give any reason for their hope, since that task belongs to experts.
Faith is exactly a leap in the dark, a switching off of the mind with the eyes closed; the unit teaches that trust should be blind and never grounded in any evidence.
Kant objected that existence is the most important property we can add to a thing, so Anselm's argument is decisive proof, and the unit rests the whole case for God upon it.
General revelation is enough to save, because creation and conscience reveal God's mercy and show how wrong is forgiven; nothing more such as special revelation is needed.
God made puppets who could never sin, because forced love is the truest love; freedom was never necessary, and the possibility of evil has nothing to do with love in the unit's answer.
The unit concedes that copying corrupted the text beyond recovery, since the New Testament has few surviving manuscripts and a very long gap to the originals, so reliability cannot be tested.
Inspiration means that Scripture is merely inspiring human thoughts and that the authors wrote entirely on their own, so there is nothing divine about it and the Holy Spirit did not move them.
The fingerprint of prophecy refers to vague horoscopes that could fit anyone; Micah, Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53 gave no specific predictions and do not converge on one life.
Paul teaches that Christianity survives as a beautiful philosophy even if the tomb is occupied, so the resurrection is not testable and the faith does not depend on any historical claim.
The unit concludes that the swoon theory is the best explanation, since a man flogged and pierced through the heart could easily roll away the stone, overpower guards and convince his followers.
If evolution is true then a Creator becomes unnecessary, because gradual natural processes explain the fine-tuning of the universe, and the board of the game needed no builder.
John 14:6 teaches that there are many ways to the Father and that Jesus is only one of them; the unit calls it the most welcome verse because it fits modern tolerance.
The refrain is that strong evidence and good arguments can always drag a man through the door and into the kingdom, so the apologist's cleverness and not the Spirit decides conversion.
